lead: A MOSFET is a capacitor made to conduct. A gate plate sits above doped silicon with a thin oxide between. Gate voltage first pushes majority carriers away, then pulls minority carriers to the surface, forming a thin channel. Source and drain turn the capacitor into a switch. Cutoff, linear and saturation describe the channel. Naming the region from terminal voltages is the first VLSI design skill.
prereq: School-level electrostatics (charge, field, capacitance) and semiconductor devices — doping, the pn junction and the depletion region.

sections.h3: The MOS capacitor: accumulation, depletion, inversion

blocks.text: A p-type body has acceptor doping N<sub>A</sub> (cm<sup>−3</sup>), so holes are majority carriers. A silicon dioxide layer of thickness t<sub>ox</sub>, a few nanometres, covers the surface. A polysilicon or metal gate on the oxide forms a parallel-plate capacitor with the body.
V<sub>FB</sub> is the gate-to-body voltage with flat bands and no surface charge. Measure gate voltage V<sub>G</sub> from there.

Below VFB, the negative gate attracts holes into accumulation. Above VFB, the positive gate repels holes; a depletion region of ionised acceptors widens to width Wd. The surface potential φs (V) is the band bending and grows with VG.

Electrons, minority carriers in p-type silicon, are attracted to the positive gate. When φs reaches 2φF, surface electron concentration equals bulk hole concentration: the surface has inverted to n-type. This thin n-type sheet is the channel; the gate voltage where it first appears is VT.

blocks.where: φ<sub>F</sub> is bulk Fermi potential (V); k = 1.38×10<sup>−23</sup> J/K is Boltzmann's constant; T is temperature (K, 300 K at room); q = 1.6×10<sup>−19</sup> C is electron charge; N<sub>A</sub> is acceptor doping (cm<sup>−3</sup>); n<sub>i</sub> ≈ 10<sup>10</sup> cm<sup>−3</sup> for silicon. Inversion starts at surface potential 2φ<sub>F</sub>.

sections.h3: From capacitor to transistor: the channel appears

blocks.text: Add two n<sup>+</sup> source and drain regions in the p body on either side of the gate. Terminals: gate (G), source (S), drain (D), body (B). Carriers enter at the source; source and body are usually tied.

With V<sub>GS</sub> > 0 and V<sub>DS</sub> = 0, the inverted sheet joins the n<sup>+</sup> regions once V<sub>GS</sub> > V<sub>T</sub>. The excess V<sub>OV</sub> = V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub> buys inversion charge.

With V<sub>DS</sub> > 0, channel potential rises from 0 at source to V<sub>DS</sub> at drain. Gate-to-channel voltage is V<sub>GS</sub> at source and V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>DS</sub> at drain. Inversion charge follows local gate-to-channel voltage minus V<sub>T</sub>, so the channel is thick at source and thin at drain.

Increasing VDS thins the drain end. It vanishes at VGS − VDS = VT, that is VDS = VGS − VT: pinch-off. Beyond it, extra voltage drops across a short depleted region near the drain and current stays almost flat; the gate feels only overdrive.

sections.h3: The three regions, nMOS and pMOS

blocks.text: Cutoff: no channel, only leakage (see 1.7). Linear: continuous channel; gate-controlled resistor (also called triode or ohmic in some syllabi). Saturation: channel pinched off at drain; current source set by VGS.

A pMOS flips signs: n-type body, p<sup>+</sup> source and drain, holes form the channel. Source is the higher potential, so V<sub>GS</sub>, V<sub>DS</sub> and V<sub>T</sub> are negative. Habit: compare magnitudes |V<sub>GS</sub>| with |V<sub>T</sub>|, and |V<sub>DS</sub>| with |V<sub>GS</sub>| − |V<sub>T</sub>|.

spec.title: Choosing the nMOS region
spec.aria: A decision chart that names the nMOS region from the terminal voltages: cutoff when the gate voltage is below the threshold, otherwise linear when drain voltage is below the overdrive, otherwise saturation.

examples.question: An nMOS has V<sub>T</sub> = 0.5 V, k<sub>n</sub>′ = 100 µA/V² and W/L = 10. (a) With V<sub>GS</sub> = 1.5 V and V<sub>DS</sub> = 0.4 V, find the region and drain current. (b) V<sub>GS</sub> stays at 1.5 V and V<sub>DS</sub> rises to 1.5 V; find the region and drain current. k<sub>n</sub>′ = µ<sub>n</sub>C<sub>ox</sub> is the process transconductance parameter.
steps: Overdrive V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub> = 1.0 V, positive, so not cutoff.
(b) V<sub>DS</sub> = 1.5 V > 1.0 V: saturation at V<sub>DS</sub> = 1.0 V.
examples.answer: (a) Linear region with I<sub>D</sub> = 320 µA; (b) saturation region with I<sub>D</sub> = 500 µA.

traps: Swapping nMOS and pMOS tests. A pMOS conducts when V<sub>GS</sub> is more negative than V<sub>T</sub>; compare magnitudes.
Using excess above overdrive in the region test. The V<sub>DS</sub> in the test is the full drain-to-source voltage, not V<sub>DS</sub> − (V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>).
Forgetting that V<sub>DS</sub> on a pMOS is negative when the source is the higher terminal.
Believing the channel vanishes at pinch-off. Only the drain end pinches; current continues, set by overdrive.
Treating V<sub>T</sub> as turn-on for useful current. V<sub>T</sub> is where the channel first forms; real current needs V<sub>GS</sub> comfortably above it.

quiz.q: Name the three states of the MOS capacitor with a p-type body as V<sub>G</sub> moves from below V<sub>FB</sub> upward, and give the condition for each.
quiz.a: Accumulation: V<sub>G</sub> < V<sub>FB</sub>, holes pile at the surface. Depletion: V<sub>G</sub> > V<sub>FB</sub>, holes are pushed away and a depletion region of width W<sub>d</sub> opens. Inversion: surface potential reaches 2φ<sub>F</sub> and an electron channel forms.

quiz.q: Write the region tests for an nMOS in terms of V<sub>GS</sub>, V<sub>DS</sub> and V<sub>T</sub>.
quiz.a: Cutoff: V<sub>GS</sub> < V<sub>T</sub>. Linear: V<sub>GS</sub> > V<sub>T</sub> and V<sub>DS</sub> < V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>. Saturation: V<sub>GS</sub> > V<sub>T</sub> and V<sub>DS</sub> ≥ V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>.

quiz.q: Why does inversion begin at a surface potential of 2φ<sub>F</sub> rather than φ<sub>F</sub>?
quiz.a: φ<sub>F</sub> is the distance from the intrinsic level to the bulk Fermi level. Bending the bands by φ<sub>F</sub> brings the surface to intrinsic condition. A further φ<sub>F</sub> raises surface electron concentration to N<sub>A</sub>, matching bulk hole concentration, so strong inversion begins.

quiz.q: Why does the drain end of the channel pinch off before the source end?
quiz.a: Channel potential rises from 0 at source to V<sub>DS</sub> at drain, so gate-to-channel voltage is smallest at drain, V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>DS</sub>. Inversion charge follows that voltage minus V<sub>T</sub>, so the channel thins toward the drain and reaches zero when V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>DS</sub> = V<sub>T</sub>.

quiz.q: An nMOS has V<sub>T</sub> = 0.6 V and k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L) = 500 µA/V². With V<sub>GS</sub> = 1.6 V and V<sub>DS</sub> = 0.5 V, find the region and I<sub>D</sub>.
quiz.a: Overdrive = 1.6 − 0.6 = 1.0 V, positive, so not cutoff. V<sub>DS</sub> = 0.5 V < 1.0 V, so linear. I<sub>D</sub> = 500 µA/V² × [(1.0 V)(0.5 V) − (0.5 V)²/2] = 500 × 0.375 µA = 187.5 µA.

quiz.q: A pMOS has V<sub>T</sub> = −0.5 V. With V<sub>GS</sub> = −1.2 V and V<sub>DS</sub> = −0.3 V, which region is it in?
quiz.a: |V<sub>GS</sub>| = 1.2 V > |V<sub>T</sub>| = 0.5 V, so a channel exists. Overdrive magnitude = 0.7 V; |V<sub>DS</sub>| = 0.3 V < 0.7 V, so linear (triode).

quiz.q: An nMOS with V<sub>T</sub> = 0.5 V and k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L) = 1000 µA/V² is held at V<sub>GS</sub> = 1.5 V while V<sub>DS</sub> sweeps from 0 V to 2 V. Explain how I<sub>D</sub> behaves.
quiz.a: Up to V<sub>DS</sub> = 1.0 V = V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub> the device is linear and I<sub>D</sub> rises as 1000 × (1.0 V<sub>DS</sub> − V<sub>DS</sub>²/2) µA, flattening near pinch-off. At V<sub>DS</sub> = 1.0 V, I<sub>D</sub> = 500 µA. Beyond it the device is in saturation and I<sub>D</sub> stays at 500 µA, idealised as a flat line.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real design kits use compact models such as BSIM, with many parameters a single V<sub>T</sub> cannot capture. The three-state picture underlies surface-potential and charge-sheet models. In advanced nodes the planar body becomes a fin or gate-all-around nanosheet, but the same question decides the region: has the gate inverted the surface, and is the drain end pinched off?
